Fatma Aysazcı Çakar* Abstract: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a serious mental health condition in which individuals develop physical and psychological symptoms following traumatic experiences. Various therapeutic approaches are currently used in the treatment of it, with Cognitive Behavioral Therapies and Prolonged Exposure Therapy being among the most empirically supported methods.

In recent years, however, Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) has emerged as a promising approach, particularly for treating complex trauma. The purpose of this article is to explain the theoretical foundations of NET, a trauma-focused approach widely used worldwide, to evaluate its effectiveness through literature review, and to increase its use by experts and in Türkiye.

NET is a holistic therapeutic model that aims to help individuals process traumatic events in a safe environment by chronologically structuring their life narratives. This method integrates multiple techniques, including exposure therapy, testimony therapy, and autobiographical memory reprocessing. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of NET in reducing PTSD symptoms among refugees, war survivors, torture victims, and domestic violence survivors.

Additionally, it has been successfully applied to a broader population, including natural disaster victims, individuals with childhood trauma, survivors of sexual violence, and offenders. The implementation of NET involves constructing a life timeline, symbolizing life events using flowers and stones, detailing traumatic experiences, and engaging in therapeutic reconstruction processes.

With its structured and time-limited format, NET is considered a viable option for both clinical and field applications. It is particularly valuable in high-trauma regions and for professionals working with limited resources. This study explores the theoretical foundations, application process, and effectiveness of NET, discussing its potential as an alternative approach for PTSD treatment. Furthermore, the importance of expanding its use in Turkiye is emphasized.

Bu kuramsal makalenin amacı; Dünya genelinde yaygın olarak kullanılan travma odaklı bir yaklaşım olan NET’in teorik temellerinin açıklanması, literatürdeki çalışmalarla etkiliğinin değerlendirilmesi, tekniğin uygulanması ve Türkiye’de kullanımının yaygınlaştırılmasının önemini tartışmaktır. NET, bireylerin yaşam öyküsünü kronolojik olarak yapılandırarak, travmatik olayları güvenli bir ortamda tekrar işlemelerini sağlamayı amaçlayan bütüncül bir terapi modelidir.

Bu yöntem; maruz bırakma teknikleri, şahitlik terapisi ve otobiyografik belleği yeniden işleme gibi farklı teknikleri birleştirerek kullanmaktadır. Araştırmalar, NET’in mülteciler, savaş mağdurları, işkence gören bireyler ve aile içi şiddet mağdurları gibi gruplarda TSSB semptomlarını azaltmada etkili olduğunu göstermektedir.

Ayrıca, doğal afet mağdurları, çocukluk çağı travması yaşayan bireyler, cinsel şiddet mağdurları ve suç failleri gibi geniş bir popülasyonda da başarılı olduğu kanıtlanmıştır. NET’in uygulanışı; bireyin yaşam çizgisinin oluşturulması, yaşam olaylarının çiçek ve taşlarla sembolleştirilmesi, travmatik olayların detaylandırılması ve terapötik yeniden yapılandırma süreçlerini içermektedir.

Teknik, kısa süreli ve standardize edilmiş yapısıyla hem klinik hem de saha uygulamaları için uygun bir seçenek sunmaktadır. Özellikle travmanın yoğun olduğu bölgelerde ve sınırlı kaynaklarla çalışan profesyoneller için etkili bir müdahale aracı olarak değerlendirilmektedir. Bu çalışmada ise; NET’in teorik temelleri, uygulama süreci ve etkililiği ele alınarak, TSSB tedavisinde nasıl bir alternatif sunduğu tartışılmıştır.
Özellikle Türkiye’deki uygulamalar açısından bu yöntemin yaygınlaştırılmasının önemi vurgulanmaktadır.

Structured Abstract: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a debilitating mental health condition that arises following exposure to traumatic events, often resulting in persistent psychological and physiological symptoms. Traditional therapeutic approaches such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Prolonged Exposure Therapy (PE) have long been considered gold-standard treatments for PTSD.

However, recent years have witnessed the emergence of Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) as a promising alternative, particularly for individuals with complex trauma histories and those living in high-trauma regions with limited access to mental health resources.

NET is a structured, short-term, and integrative therapeutic model that combines principles from CBT, testimony therapy, client-centered psychotherapy, and neurotraumatology. Its core objective is to help individuals reconstruct their autobiographical memory by integrating traumatic experiences into a coherent life narrative.

This is achieved through a symbolic and ritualized process involving the construction of a “lifeline,” where life events are represented using physical symbols chronologically—flowers for positive experiences and stones for traumatic ones. This method does not only facilitate emotional processing but also empowers individuals to reclaim agency over their life stories.

The theoretical foundation of NET is rooted in the Dual Representation Theory of Memory, which posits that traumatic memories are stored in two distinct systems: “hot” memory (emotional and sensory components) and “cold” memory (contextual and factual details). Traumatic experiences often disrupt the integration of these systems, leading to fragmented and intrusive recollections.

NET aims to reprocess these memories by activating both systems in a safe therapeutic environment, thereby reducing PTSD symptoms and restoring narrative coherence. The therapy also draws upon the Emotional Processing Model, emphasizing the importance of habituation and cognitive restructuring in trauma recovery.

NET is implemented through four structured phases: (1) Assessment and psychoeducation, (2) Lifeline construction, (3) Narrative elaboration of life events, and (4) Final reading and consolidation. During these sessions, the therapist plays a critical role in facilitating detailed recall, maintaining emotional safety, and ensuring the integration of fragmented memories.
The process is designed to be flexible and adaptable to the individual’s trauma history, cultural background, and psychological needs.

Empirical evidence from randomized controlled trials has demonstrated the efficacy of NET across diverse populations, including refugees, survivors of war, torture, domestic violence, and natural disasters. Studies have shown significant reductions in PTSD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and stress among participants.

Adaptations of NET such as KIDNET (for children), FORNET (for offenders), and e-NET (for online delivery) further highlight the versatility and scalability of the approach. These formats have been successfully applied in various cultural contexts, including African refugee settlements, post-tsunami regions in Sri Lanka, and among survivors of political imprisonment in Eastern Europe.

In the context of Türkiye, where exposure to trauma is prevalent due to natural disasters, migration, and socio-political factors, NET holds significant potential. Despite its proven effectiveness, the application of NET in Türkiye remains limited. Preliminary research involving Syrian refugees has shown promising results, indicating reductions in PTSD, depression, anxiety, and improvements in self-concept clarity.
These findings underscore the need for further research, cultural adaptation, and dissemination of NET in clinical and community settings across the country.

The article concludes by emphasizing the importance of expanding NET’s use in Türkiye, particularly in regions with high trauma exposure and limited mental health infrastructure. It advocates for the integration of NET into public health systems, training of mental health professionals, and the development of culturally sensitive protocols to enhance its accessibility and effectiveness.

By doing so, NET can serve as a valuable tool in addressing the psychological aftermath of trauma and promoting resilience among affected populations. Keywords: Psychology, Narrative Exposure Therapy, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, Trauma-Focused Interventions, Psychological Counseling.

االستشارة النفسية. Résumé structuré: Le syndrome de stress post-traumatique (SSPT) est un trouble mental invalidant qui survient à la suite d'une exposition à des événements traumatisants et qui entraîne souvent des symptômes psychologiques et physiologiques persistants.

Les approches thérapeutiques traditionnelles telles que la thérapie cognitivocomportementale (TCC) et la thérapie par exposition prolongée (PE) ont longtemps été considérées comme les traitements de référence pour le SSPT.

Cependant, ces dernières années ont vu l'émergence de la thérapie par exposition narrative (TEN) comme une alternative prometteuse, en particulier pour les personnes ayant des antécédents traumatiques complexes et celles vivant dans des régions à fort taux de traumatismes avec un accès limité aux ressources en santé mentale.

La TEN est un modèle thérapeutique structuré, à court terme et intégratif qui combine les principes de la TCC, de la thérapie par le témoignage, de la psychothérapie centrée sur le client et de la neurotraumatologie. Son objectif principal est d'aider les individus à reconstruire leur mémoire autobiographique en intégrant leurs expériences traumatiques dans un récit de vie cohérent.

Pour ce faire, elle utilise un processus symbolique et ritualisé qui consiste à construire une « ligne de vie », où les événements de la vie sont représentés à l'aide de symboles physiques classés par ordre chronologique : des fleurs pour les expériences positives et des pierres pour les expériences traumatiques. Cette méthode facilite non seulement le traitement émotionnel, mais permet également aux individus de reprendre le contrôle de leur histoire personnelle.

Le fondement théorique de la NET est ancré dans la théorie de la double représentation de la mémoire, qui postule que les souvenirs traumatiques sont stockés dans deux systèmes distincts : la mémoire « chaude » (composantes émotionnelles et sensorielles) et la mémoire « froide » (détails contextuels et factuels). Les expériences traumatiques perturbent souvent l'intégration de ces systèmes, entraînant des souvenirs fragmentés et intrusifs.

La NET vise à retraiter ces souvenirs en activant les deux systèmes dans un environnement thérapeutique sûr, réduisant ainsi les symptômes du SSPT et rétablissant la cohérence narrative. La thérapie s'appuie également sur le modèle de traitement émotionnel, qui souligne l'importance de l'accoutumance et de la restructuration cognitive dans le rétablissement après un traumatisme.

La NET est mise en œuvre en quatre phases structurées : (1) Évaluation et psychoéducation, (2) Construction d'une ligne de vie, (3) Élaboration narrative des événements de la vie, et (4) Lecture finale et consolidation. Au cours de ces séances, le thérapeute joue un rôle essentiel en facilitant le rappel détaillé, en maintenant la sécurité émotionnelle et en assurant l'intégration des souvenirs fragmentés.
Le processus est conçu pour être flexible et adaptable à l'histoire traumatique, au contexte culturel et aux besoins psychologiques de chaque individu.

Des preuves empiriques issues d'essais contrôlés randomisés ont démontré l'efficacité de la NET auprès de diverses populations, notamment les réfugiés, les survivants de la guerre, de la torture, de la violence domestique et des catastrophes naturelles. Des études ont montré une réduction significative des symptômes du SSPT, de la dépression, de l'anxiété et du stress chez les participants.

Les adaptations de la NET telles que KIDNET (pour les enfants), FORNET (pour les délinquants) et e-NET (pour la prestation en ligne) soulignent encore davantage la polyvalence et l'évolutivité de l'approche. Ces formats ont été appliqués avec succès dans divers contextes culturels, notamment dans les camps de réfugiés africains, dans les régions touchées par le tsunami au Sri Lanka et parmi les survivants d'emprisonnement politique en Europe de l'Est.

Dans le contexte de la Turquie, où l'exposition aux traumatismes est fréquente en raison des catastrophes naturelles, des migrations et des facteurs sociopolitiques, la NET présente un potentiel important. Malgré son efficacité prouvée, l'application de la NET en Turquie reste limitée.

Des recherches préliminaires menées auprès de réfugiés syriens ont donné des résultats prometteurs, indiquant une réduction du syndrome de stress post-traumatique, de la dépression et de l'anxiété, ainsi qu'une amélioration de la clarté du concept de soi. Ces résultats soulignent la nécessité de poursuivre les recherches, l'adaptation culturelle et la diffusion de la NET dans les milieux cliniques et communautaires à travers le pays.

L'article conclut en soulignant l'importance d'étendre l'utilisation de la NET en Turquie, en particulier dans les régions où l'exposition aux traumatismes est élevée et où les infrastructures de santé mentale sont limitées. Il préconise l'intégration de la NET dans les systèmes de santé publique, la formation des professionnels de la santé mentale et l'élaboration de protocoles adaptés à la culture afin d'améliorer son accessibilité et son efficacité.
Ce faisant, la NET peut constituer un outil précieux pour traiter les séquelles psychologiques des traumatismes et promouvoir la résilience parmi les populations touchées.

Resumen Estructurado: El trastorno por estrés postraumático (TEPT) es una afección de salud mental debilitante que surge tras la exposición a eventos traumáticos y que a menudo provoca síntomas psicológicos y fisiológicos persistentes. Los enfoques terapéuticos tradicionales, como la terapia cognitivo-conductual (TCC) y la terapia de exposición prolongada (PE), se han considerado durante mucho tiempo los tratamientos de referencia para el TEPT.

Sin embargo, en los últimos años ha surgido la terapia de exposición narrativa (TEN) como una alternativa prometedora, especialmente para personas con historiales traumáticos complejos y aquellas que viven en regiones con altos índices de trauma y acceso limitado a recursos de salud mental.

La TEN es un modelo terapéutico estructurado, a corto plazo e integrador que combina principios de la TCC, la terapia del testimonio, la psicoterapia centrada en el cliente y la neurotraumatología. Su objetivo principal es ayudar a las personas a reconstruir su memoria autobiográfica integrando las experiencias traumáticas en una narrativa coherente de su vida.

Esto se consigue mediante un proceso simbólico y ritualizado que implica la construcción de una «línea de vida», en la que los acontecimientos vitales se representan cronológicamente mediante símbolos físicos: flores para las experiencias positivas y piedras para las traumáticas. Este método no solo facilita el procesamiento emocional, sino que también empodera a las personas para que recuperen el control sobre sus historias de vida.

La base teórica de la NET se fundamenta en la teoría de la doble representación de la memoria, que postula que los recuerdos traumáticos se almacenan en dos sistemas distintos: la memoria «caliente» (componentes emocionales y sensoriales) y la memoria «fría» (detalles contextuales y fácticos). Las experiencias traumáticas a menudo alteran la integración de estos sistemas, lo que da lugar a recuerdos fragmentados e intrusivos.

La NET tiene como objetivo reprocesar estos recuerdos activando ambos sistemas en un entorno terapéutico seguro, reduciendo así los síntomas del TEPT y restaurando la coherencia narrativa. La terapia también se basa en el modelo de procesamiento emocional, que enfatiza la importancia de la habituación y la reestructuración cognitiva en la recuperación del trauma.

La NET se implementa a través de cuatro fases estructuradas: (1) Evaluación y psicoeducación, (2) Construcción de una línea de vida, (3) Elaboración narrativa de los acontecimientos de la vida, y (4) Lectura final y consolidación. Durante estas sesiones, el terapeuta desempeña un papel fundamental a la hora de facilitar el recuerdo detallado, mantener la seguridad emocional y garantizar la integración de los recuerdos fragmentados.
El proceso está diseñado para ser flexible y adaptable al historial traumático, los antecedentes culturales y las necesidades psicológicas de cada persona.

Las pruebas empíricas de ensayos controlados aleatorios han demostrado la eficacia de la NET en diversas poblaciones, incluyendo refugiados, supervivientes de guerras, torturas, violencia doméstica y desastres naturales. Los estudios han demostrado una reducción significativa de los síntomas de TEPT, depresión, ansiedad y estrés entre los participantes.

Las adaptaciones de la NET, como KIDNET (para niños), FORNET (para delincuentes) y e-NET (para la prestación de servicios en línea), ponen aún más de relieve la versatilidad y la escalabilidad de este enfoque. Estos formatos se han aplicado con éxito en diversos contextos culturales, como los asentamientos de refugiados africanos, las regiones afectadas por el tsunami en Sri Lanka y entre los supervivientes de encarcelamientos políticos en Europa del Este.

En el contexto de Turquía, donde la exposición al trauma es frecuente debido a los desastres naturales, la migración y los factores sociopolíticos, la NET tiene un potencial significativo. A pesar de su eficacia demostrada, la aplicación de la NET en Turquía sigue siendo limitada.

Las investigaciones preliminares con refugiados sirios han mostrado resultados prometedores, que indican una reducción del trastorno de estrés postraumático, la depresión y la ansiedad, así como una mejora en la claridad del concepto de uno mismo. Estos hallazgos subrayan la necesidad de seguir investigando, adaptando culturalmente y difundiendo la NET en entornos clínicos y comunitarios de todo el país.

El artículo concluye haciendo hincapié en la importancia de ampliar el uso de la NET en Turquía, especialmente en regiones con alta exposición al trauma y una infraestructura de salud mental limitada. Aboga por la integración de la NET en los sistemas de salud pública, la formación de profesionales de la salud mental y el desarrollo de protocolos culturalmente sensibles para mejorar su accesibilidad y eficacia.
De este modo, la NET puede servir como una herramienta valiosa para abordar las secuelas psicológicas del trauma y promover la resiliencia entre las poblaciones afectadas.

结构化摘要： 创伤后应激障碍（PTSD）是一种因暴露于创伤事件后引发的严重精神健康问题，常导致持 续性心理及生理症状。认知行为疗法（CBT）和持续暴露疗法（PE）等传统治疗手段长期被视为 PTSD的金标准疗法。然而近年来，叙事暴露疗法（NET）作为一种充满希望的替代方案应运而生， 尤其适用于具有复杂创伤史的个体以及生活在高创伤地区且心理健康资源有限的人群。 NET是一种结构化、短期、综合性的治疗模式，融合了CBT、证词疗法、以客户为中心的心 理治疗和神经创伤学原理。其核心目标是通过将创伤经历融入连贯的人生叙事，帮助个体重建自传 体记忆。该疗法采用象征性仪式化过程——构建“生命线”，以实体符号按时间顺序呈现人生事件：鲜 花代表积极经历，石块象征创伤体验。这种方法不仅促进情感处理，更赋予个体重获人生叙事主导 权的力量。 NET的理论根基植于记忆双重表征理论，该理论认为创伤记忆存储于两个独立系统：“热”记 忆（情感与感官成分）和“冷”记忆（情境与事实细节）。创伤经历常导致这两套系统整合失调，引发 片段化与侵入性回忆。NET旨在通过在安全治疗环境中激活双系统来重构记忆，从而减轻PTSD症状 并恢复叙事连贯性。该疗法同时借鉴情绪处理模型，强调习惯化和认知重构在创伤康复中的重要性 。 NET通过四个结构化阶段实施：（1）评估与心理教育；（2）生命线构建；（3）人生事件 叙事详述；（4）最终阅读与巩固。治疗师在会谈中扮演关键角色，负责引导详细回忆、维持情绪安 全感并确保碎片化记忆整合。该过程设计灵活，可适应个体创伤史、文化背景及心理需求。 随机对照试验的实证研究证实，NET在难民、战争幸存者、酷刑受害者、家暴幸存者及自然 灾害幸存者等多元群体中均具疗效。研究显示参与者创伤后应激障碍症状、抑郁、焦虑及压力水平 显著降低。NET衍生方案如儿童版KIDNET、罪犯版FORNET及在线版e-NET，进一步彰显了该疗法 的普适性与可扩展性。这些模式已在非洲难民营、斯里兰卡海啸灾区、东欧政治囚犯群体等多元文 化环境中成功实施。 在土耳其，由于自然灾害、移民潮及社会政治因素导致创伤暴露普遍，NET具有巨大应用潜 力。尽管疗效确凿，该疗法在土耳其的应用仍受限。针对叙利亚难民的初步研究显示出积极成效： 创伤后应激障碍、抑郁、焦虑症状显著减轻，自我概念清晰度得到提升。这些发现强调了在土耳其 全国临床及社区环境中推进NET研究、文化适应与推广的必要性。 文章最后着重指出，应在土耳其创伤暴露率高且心理健康基础设施薄弱的地区扩大NET应用 范围。文章倡导将NET纳入公共卫生体系，培训心理健康专业人员，并制定文化敏感性协议以提升其 可及性与有效性。通过这些举措，NET可成为应对创伤心理后遗症、促进受影响人群韧性的重要工具 。 关键词：心理学，叙事暴露疗法，创伤后应激障碍，创伤聚焦干预，心理咨询。 Структурированное резюме:

Однако в последние годы появилась нарративная

NET реализуется в четыре этапа: (1) оценка и психообразование, (2) построение линии жизни, (3) нарративная проработка жизненных событий и (4) окончательное прочтение и консолидация. Во время этих сессий терапевт играет важную роль в содействии детальному воспоминанию, поддержании эмоциональной безопасности и обеспечении интеграции фрагментированных воспоминаний.
Процесс разработан так, чтобы быть гибким и адаптируемым к истории травмы, культурному контексту и психологическим потребностям каждого человека.

Эмпирические данные рандомизированных контролируемых испытаний продемонстрировали эффективность NET среди различных групп населения, включая беженцев, выживших после войны, пыток, домашнего насилия и стихийных бедствий. Исследования показали значительное снижение симптомов ПТСР, депрессии, тревоги и стресса среди участников.

Адаптации NET, такие как KIDNET (для детей), FORNET (для правонарушителей) и e-NET (для онлайн-доставки), еще больше подчеркивают универсальность и масштабируемость этого подхода. Эти форматы были успешно применены в различных культурных контекстах, включая африканские поселения беженцев, регионы Шри-Ланки, пострадавшие от цунами, и среди выживших после политического заключения в Восточной Европе.

В контексте Турции, где травматические переживания являются распространенным явлением из-за стихийных бедствий, миграции и социально-политических факторов, NET имеет значительный потенциал. Несмотря на доказанную эффективность, применение NET в Турции остается ограниченным. Предварительные исследования с участием сирийских беженцев показали обнадеживающие результаты, свидетельствующие о снижении уровня ПТСР, депрессии, тревоги и улучшении ясности самооценки.
Эти результаты подчеркивают необходимость дальнейших исследований, культурной адаптации и распространения NET в клинических и общественных учреждениях по всей стране.

В заключение статьи подчеркивается важность расширения использования NET в Турции, особенно в регионах с высоким уровнем травматизации и ограниченной инфраструктурой психического здоровья. В ней отстаивается интеграция NET в системы общественного здравоохранения, обучение специалистов в области психического здоровья и разработка протоколов, учитывающих культурные особенности, для повышения ее доступности и эффективности.
Таким образом, NET может служить ценным инструментом в устранении психологических последствий травм и укреплении устойчивости среди пострадавшего населения.

संरचित सार पोस्ट-ट्रॉमेटट्क स्टरेस टिसऑिडर (PTSD) एक गंभीर मानटसक स्वास्थ्य टिकार है, जो प्रायः आघातपूर्ड घट्नाओं के संपकड में आने के बाद उत्पन्न होता है और लंबे समय तक बने रहने िाले मनोिैज्ञाटनक तथा शारीररक लक्षर्ों का कारर् बनता है। पारंपररक उपचार पद्धटतयााँ, जैसे टक कॉटिटट्ि टबहेटियरल थेरेपी (CBT) और प्रोलॉन्ग्ि एक्सपोज़र थेरेपी (PE), लंबे समय से PTSD के टलए स्वर्ड-मानक उपचार मानी जाती रही हैं। तथाटप,

हाल के िर्षों में नैरेटट्ि एक्सपोज़र थेरेपी (NET) एक प्रभािशाली िैकल्पिक पद्धटत के रूप में उभरी है, टिशेर्षकर उन व्यल्पियों के टलए टजनका आघात इटतहास जटट्ल रहा है तथा जो उच्च-आघात िाले क्षेत्ों में रहते हैं, जहााँ मानटसक स्वास्थ्य संसाधनों तक पहाँच सीटमत है। NET एक संरटचत, अिकाटलक और समल्पित टचटकत्सीय मॉिल है, जो CBT, ट्ेल्पस्टमनी थेरेपी,

क्लाइंट्-केंटित मनोटचटकत्सा तथा न्यूरोट्रॉमेट्ोलॉजी के टसद्धांतों को एकीकृत करता है। इसका मुख्य उद्देश्य व्यल्पियों को उनकी आत्मकथात्मक स्मृटतयों का पुनटनडमाडर् करने में सहायता करना है, ताटक आघातपूर्ड अनुभिों को एक संगत जीिन-कथा में समाटहत टकया जा सके। यह प्रटिया “लाइफलाइन” नामक एक प्रतीकात्मक और अनुष्ठाटनक पद्धटत के माध्यम से संपन्न की जाती है,

टजसमें जीिन की घट्नाओं को कालानुिटमक िम में भौटतक प्रतीकों द्वारा दशाडया जाता है—सकारात्मक अनुभिों के टलए फूल और आघातपूर्ड अनुभिों के टलए पत्थर। यह टिटध न केिल भािनात्मक प्रसंस्करर् को सुगम बनाती है, बल्पि व्यल्पियों को अपनी जीिन-कथा पर पुनः टनयंत्र् और स्वायत्तता प्राप्त करने में भी सशि करती है। NET का सैद्धांटतक आधार स्मृटत की टद्व-प्रटतटनटधत्व टसद्धांत (Dual Representation Theory of Memory) में टनटहत है,

टजसके अनुसार आघात संबंधी स्मृटतयााँ दो पृथक प्रर्ाटलयों में संग्रहीत होती हैं: “हॉट्” स्मृटत (भािनात्मक और संिेदनात्मक घट्क) और “कोल्ड” स्मृटत (प्रासंटगक और तथ्यात्मक टििरर्)। आघातपूर्ड अनुभि प्रायः इन दोनों प्रर्ाटलयों के एकीकरर् को बाटधत कर देते हैं, टजसके पररर्ामस्वरूप स्मृटतयााँ खंटित और अनैल्पिक रूप से पुनः उभरने लगती हैं। NET का उद्देश्य एक सुरटक्षत टचटकत्सीय िातािरर् में दोनों प्रर्ाटलयों को सटिय कर इन स्मृटतयों का पुनःप्रसंस्करर् करना है,

टजससे PTSD के लक्षर्ों में कमी आए और जीिन-कथा की संगटत पुनः स्थाटपत हो। यह थेरेपी भािनात्मक प्रसंस्करर् मॉिल (Emotional Processing Model) पर भी आधाररत है, जो आघात से उबरने की प्रटिया में अभ्यस्तता (habituation) और संज्ञानात्मक पुनगडठन (cognitive restructuring) के महत्व को रेखांटकत करता है। NET को चार संरटचत चरर्ों के माध्यम से लागू टकया जाता है: (1) मूल्ांकन और मनो-टशक्षा, (2) लाइफलाइन का टनमाडर्, (3) जीिन-घट्नाओं का कथात्मक टिस्तार,

और (4) अंटतम िाचन और समेकन। इन सत्ों के दौरान टचटकत्सक की भूटमका अत्यंत महत्वपूर्ड होती है, टजसमें टिस्तृत स्मृटत-पुनःस्मरर् को सुगम बनाना, भािनात्मक सुरक्षा बनाए रखना, और खंटित स्मृटतयों के एकीकरर् को सुटनटित करना शाटमल है। यह प्रटिया व्यल्पि के आघात इटतहास, सांस्कृटतक पृष्ठभूटम और मनोिैज्ञाटनक आिश्यकताओं के अनुसार लचीली और अनुकूलनीय रूप से टिज़ाइन की जाती है। यादृल्पिक टनयंटत्त परीक्षर्ों (randomized controlled trials) से प्राप्त अनुभिजन्य प्रमार्ों ने शरर्ाटथडयों,

युद्ध और यातना के पीट़ितों, घरेलू टहंसा से बचे व्यल्पियों तथा प्राकृटतक आपदाओं से प्रभाटित लोगों सटहत टिटिध जनसंख्याओं में NET की प्रभािशीलता को टसद्ध टकया है। शोधों में प्रटतभाटगयों के PTSD लक्षर्ों, अिसाद, टचंता और तनाि में उल्लेखनीय कमी पाई गई है। NET के टिटभन्न अनुकूटलत रूप, जैसे KIDNET (बच्चों के टलए), FORNET (अपराटधयों के टलए), और e-NET (ऑनलाइन माध्यम के टलए),

इस पद्धटत की बहपयोटगता और टिस्तार-क्षमता को और स्पष्ट करते हैं। इन प्रारूपों का सफलतापूिडक टिटभन्न सांस्कृटतक संदभों में उपयोग टकया गया है, जैसे अफ्रीकी शरर्ाथी टशटिर, श्रीलंका के सुनामी-पिात क्षेत्, तथा पूिी यूरोप में राजनीटतक कारािास से बचे व्यल्पियों के बीच। तुटकडये के संदभड में, जहााँ प्राकृटतक आपदाओं, प्रिास और सामाटजक-राजनीटतक कारकों के कारर् आघात का अनुभि व्यापक है, NET अत्यंत संभािनाशील दृटष्टकोर् प्रस्तुत करती है। इसके टसद्ध प्रभाि के बािजूद,

तुटकडये में NET का अनुप्रयोग अभी भी सीटमत है। सीररयाई शरर्ाटथडयों पर टकए गए प्रारंटभक शोधों ने आशाजनक पररर्ाम दशाडए हैं, टजनमें PTSD, अिसाद और टचंता के स्तर में कमी तथा आत्म-धारर्ा की स्पष्टता में सुधार देखा गया है। ये टनष्कर्षड देशभर के नैदाटनक और सामुदाटयक पररिेश में NET के आगे के अनुसंधान, सांस्कृटतक अनुकूलन और व्यापक प्रसार की आिश्यकता को रेखांटकत करते हैं।

NET आघात के मनोिैज्ञाटनक प्रभािों से टनपट्ने तथा प्रभाटित समुदायों में लचीलापन (resilience) टिकटसत करने के टलए एक महत्वपूर्ड उपकरर् के रूप में कायड कर सकती है। मुख्य शब्द : मनोटिज्ञान, नैरेटट्ि एक्सपोज़र थेरेपी, पोस्ट-ट्रॉमेटट्क स्टरेस टिसऑिडर, आघात-केंटित हस्तक्षेप, मनोिैज्ञाटनक परामशड। Yapılandırılmış Özet: Travma Sonrası Stres Bozukluğu (TSSB), travmatik olaylara maruz kalmanın ardından ortaya çıkan ve genellikle kalıcı psikolojik ve fizyolojik semptomlara yol açan,

zayıflatıcı bir ruh sağlığı sorunudur. Bilişsel Davranışçı Terapi (BDT) ve Uzun Süreli Maruz Kalma Terapisi (PE) gibi geleneksel terapötik yaklaşımlar, uzun süredir TSSB için altın standart tedaviler olarak kabul edilmektedir. Ancak, son yıllarda, özellikle karmaşık travma geçmişi olan bireyler ve ruh sağlığı kaynaklarına erişimi sınırlı olan yüksek travma bölgelerinde yaşayanlar için umut verici bir alternatif olarak Anlatı Maruz Kalma Terapisi (NET) ortaya çıkmıştır.

NET, CBT, tanıklık terapisi, danışan merkezli psikoterapi ve nörotravmatoloji ilkelerini birleştiren yapılandırılmış, kısa süreli ve bütünleştirici bir terapötik modeldir. Temel amacı, travmatik deneyimleri tutarlı bir yaşam öyküsüne entegre ederek bireylerin otobiyografik hafızalarını yeniden inşa etmelerine yardımcı olmaktır.

Bu, yaşam olaylarının kronolojik olarak fiziksel sembollerle temsil edildiği bir “yaşam çizgisi”nin oluşturulmasını içeren sembolik ve ritüelleştirilmiş bir süreçle gerçekleştirilir; olumlu deneyimler için çiçekler, travmatik deneyimler için taşlar kullanılır. Bu yöntem sadece duygusal işlemeyi kolaylaştırmakla kalmaz, aynı zamanda bireylerin yaşam öyküleri üzerinde kontrolü yeniden ele almalarını sağlar.

NET'in teorik temeli, travmatik anıların iki farklı sistemde depolandığını öne süren Çift Temsil Anı Teorisi'ne dayanmaktadır: “sıcak” anı (duygusal ve duyusal bileşenler) ve “soğuk” anı (bağlamsal ve olgusal ayrıntılar). Travmatik deneyimler genellikle bu sistemlerin bütünlüğünü bozar ve parçalı ve rahatsız edici anılara yol açar.

NET, güvenli bir terapötik ortamda her iki sistemi de aktive ederek bu anıları yeniden işlemek, böylece TSSB semptomlarını azaltmak ve anlatı tutarlılığını yeniden sağlamak amaçlamaktadır. Terapi ayrıca Duygusal İşleme Modelinden yararlanarak travma iyileşmesinde alışma ve bilişsel yeniden yapılandırmanın önemini vurgular.

NET, dört yapılandırılmış aşamada uygulanır: (1) Değerlendirme ve psiko-eğitim, (2) Yaşam çizgisi oluşturma, (3) Yaşam olaylarının anlatımsal detaylandırılması ve (4) Son okuma ve pekiştirme. Bu seanslar sırasında, terapist ayrıntılı hatırlamayı kolaylaştırmak, duygusal güvenliği sağlamak ve parçalanmış anıların bütünleşmesini sağlamak için kritik bir rol oynar.
Süreç, kişinin travma geçmişine, kültürel geçmişine ve psikolojik ihtiyaçlarına göre esnek ve uyarlanabilir olacak şekilde tasarlanmıştır.

Randomize kontrollü denemelerden elde edilen ampirik kanıtlar, NET'in mülteciler, savaş, işkence, aile içi şiddet ve doğal afetlerden kurtulanlar dahil olmak üzere çeşitli nüfus gruplarında etkinliğini göstermiştir. Çalışmalar, katılımcılar arasında TSSB semptomları, depresyon, anksiyete ve stresin önemli ölçüde azaldığını göstermiştir.

KIDNET (çocuklar için), FORNET (suçlular için) ve e-NET (çevrimiçi sunum için) gibi NET uyarlamaları, bu yaklaşımın çok yönlülüğünü ve ölçeklenebilirliğini daha da vurgulamaktadır. Bu formatlar, Afrika'daki mülteci yerleşim yerleri, Sri Lanka'daki tsunami sonrası bölgeler ve Doğu Avrupa'daki siyasi tutuklulardan kurtulanlar dahil olmak üzere çeşitli kültürel bağlamlarda başarıyla uygulanmıştır.

Doğal afetler, göç ve sosyo-politik faktörler nedeniyle travmaya maruz kalmanın yaygın olduğu Türkiye bağlamında, NET önemli bir potansiyele sahiptir. Kanıtlanmış etkinliğine rağmen, NET'in Türkiye'deki uygulaması sınırlı kalmaktadır. Suriyeli mültecileri kapsayan ön araştırmalar, TSSB, depresyon ve anksiyetedeki azalma ve öz kavram netliğinde iyileşme gibi umut verici sonuçlar göstermiştir.
Bu bulgular, ülke genelinde klinik ve topluluk ortamlarında NET'in daha fazla araştırılması, kültürel uyarlanması ve yaygınlaştırılması gerektiğini vurgulamaktadır.

Makale, Türkiye'de, özellikle travmaya maruz kalma oranının yüksek ve ruh sağlığı altyapısının sınırlı olduğu bölgelerde NET'in kullanımının yaygınlaştırılmasının önemini vurgulayarak son bulmaktadır. Makale, NET'in erişilebilirliğini ve etkinliğini artırmak için kamu sağlık sistemlerine entegrasyonu, ruh sağlığı profesyonellerinin eğitimi ve kültürel açıdan duyarlı protokollerin geliştirilmesini savunmaktadır.

A New and Holistic Approach to the Treatment of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: Narrative
Exposure Therapy
Introduction

Individuals exposed to traumatic and stressful life events carry both physical and deep emotional psychological scars caused by these events. These individuals are at risk of developing a range of psychological problems, primarily Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) (Briere and Scott, 2015).

The American Psychiatric Association (APA, 2013) defines PTSD as a set of criteria that emerge after traumatic experiences such as a real threat of death, serious injury, or sexual violence, and include intrusive thoughts reminiscent of the trauma, nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic experience, and emotional symptoms.
The classification of PTSD has undergone various changes over time.

In the most current version used today, DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), (APA, 2013), PTSD is classified under the heading “Trauma and Stress-Related Disorders,” whereas in the previous version, DSM-4, it was classified under the category of “Anxiety Disorders.” Furthermore, DSM-5 emphasizes the need to evaluate symptoms across a broader spectrum by removing subjective emotional responses such as fear, helplessness, and horror,

which are not experienced by all individuals with PTSD, from the diagnostic criteria. The definition, meaning, assessment, and presentation of appropriate treatment methods for PTSD have undergone many changes and developments throughout history.

In the past century, important empirical data has been presented on effective methods used in the treatment of PTSD (Foa et al, 2000). Furthermore, the effectiveness of various approaches used in PTSD treatment has been demonstrated in both individual trauma victims (accidents, injuries, life-threatening situations, sexual and physical assault, rape, serious illnesses) and collective trauma victims (refugees, asylum seekers, torture victims, mass killings, etc.).
There is strong evidence that these approaches lead to a significant reduction in symptoms and remission among these victims (for example,, Bradley et al, 2003; Nixon et al, 2012; Cowan et al, 2020).

According to assessments conducted by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, 2005), Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapies have been identified as the most effective potential treatment method for PTSD, considering different types of trauma.

Similarly, numerous scientific and evidence-based studies have demonstrated that PTSD can be effectively treated with various forms and variants of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and have accepted it as the first-line treatment for PTSD (Cukor et al, 2010, NICE 2005). Prolonged Exposure Therapy (PET), a sub-branch of CBT, is a treatment approach established in 1982 and built on the exposure principle specific to CBT (Foa, 2011).

It is considered the “gold standard” in the treatment of PTSD (Foa et al, 2007; Institute of Medicine, 2008). The primary goal of Prolonged Exposure Therapy is to reduce PTSD symptoms by confronting thoughts, memories, places, activities, and people associated with traumatic experiences “in the here and now” through the technique of “safe confrontation” (Foa et al, 2019).

Additionally, in the treatment of PTSD, the technique recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO, 2013) and developed in 1980 by psychologist Francine Shapiro, “Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing” (EMDR), is a treatment method whose effectiveness has been proven by numerous scientific studies (for example,, Marcus et al, 1997; Wilson et al, 2018).

EMDR aims to help individuals reprocess traumatic memories while encouraging them to focus on stressinducing elements related to the traumatic memory (images, thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations). This process, through structured eye movements using the “bilateral stimulation” technique, seeks to guide the individual and make the traumatic experience less distressing (Udo et al, 2022).

Over the past 30 years, many therapeutic approaches with potential effects on PTSD have been developed; numerous controlled experimental studies have demonstrated that Trauma-Focused CBT and EMDR are effective in the treatment of PTSD (NICE, 2005).

In recent years, Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET), which has gained wide application particularly in Europe and whose effectiveness has been demonstrated in both clinical and nonclinical settings, has been recognized as one of the effective methods for treating PTSD. NET was developed in 2005 by Schauer and colleagues, specifically for refugees living in post-conflict regions who have experienced complex trauma.

It is a short-term, standardized method proven effective in treating complex trauma and is a holistic therapy model that builds on the Prolonged Exposure technique of CBT while incorporating principles of Testimony Therapy, Client-Centered Psychotherapy, and Neurotraumatology approaches (Cienfuegos & Monelli, 1983; Foa & Rothbaum, 2001; Crombach & Siehl, 2018).

The developers of NET structured the technique around two main principles: (1) Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (TF-CBT) and (2) Testimony Therapy. The intervention assumes that recovery occurs in two ways: first, through habituation as in CBT, and second, through the consistent and coherent reconstruction (narration) of traumatic events as in Testimony Therapy (Neuner et al, 2002).

Based on these principles, reconstructing life events that cause individual and social stress and evoke emotions such as shame and anger, in a nonjudgmental, accepting, active, and empathic therapeutic setting, while restoring autobiographical memory, positions NET as a comprehensive model that also encompasses Client-Centered Psychotherapy and Neurotraumatology approaches (Schauer et al, 2025).

Accordingly, the aim of this theoretical article is to explain the theoretical foundations of NET—a trauma-focused approach frequently preferred in clinical research and practice worldwide—evaluate its effectiveness through literature, provide information on its application, and discuss the importance of expanding its use in Türkiye.

Narrative Exposure Therapy: Theoretical Background One of the theories explaining PTSD, the “dose-response relationship” theory, argues that the frequency and severity of PTSD-related symptoms are proportional to the frequency of traumatic events experienced and the impact they have on the individual (Mollica et al, 1998; 2004). Individuals exposed to complex trauma experience various difficulties in addition to PTSD.

These difficulties include problems such as emotional regulation deficits, relationship issues, dissociation, and somatization, which can pose serious threats to the individual’s ability to maintain functioning (Foa et al, 2000; Cloitre et al, 2011). Furthermore, many individuals with PTSD struggle to express their traumatic experiences, while these experiences can be re-lived through sensory elements associated with stress (Brewin, 2014).

Based on this, NET is built upon the “Dual Representation” theory of traumatic memory (Brewin et al, 2010; Schauer et al, 2024). According to the Dual Representation theory of traumatic memory, distressing symptoms related to the traumatic event arise from the interaction between autobiographical memory, intrusive thoughts, and Fear Networks.

Autobiographical memory is the type of memory in which places, time, context, content, perceptions, physical sensations, thoughts, and emotions associated with events and experiences are encoded (Tulving, 1972). Fear Networks, as defined by Lang (1977), propose that each new traumatic experience triggers similar memory structures. This model divides memory into two types: Declarative “Cold” Memory and Non-Declarative “Hot” Memory.

Declarative Cold Memory encodes contextual information related to life events (such as place, time, and context), while Non-Declarative Hot Memory records sensory, emotional, and physiological information associated with the event (Lang, 1979; Foa & Kozak, 1986).

According to the Emotional Processing Model developed by Foa and Kozak (1986), when an individual experiences a traumatic event, sensory information related to the event cannot be functionally processed into the memory system.

This leads to sensory, physical, and emotional information associated with the event remaining vivid and intense for a long time, ultimately resulting in the emergence of PTSD symptoms such as intrusive thoughts, isolation, avoidance of trauma-related cues, and flashbacks.

More specifically, during traumatic and stressful experiences, the amygdala—the region of the brain responsible for stress responses—shows hyperactivation, which helps shape appropriate stress reactions (Elbert & Schauer, 2002). The amygdala, as part of the limbic system, is also responsible for encoding information related to Non-Declarative “Hot” Memory in autobiographical memory (such as bodily sensations and thoughts associated with the event) (Conway & Fthenaki, 2000).

On the other hand, the hippocampus, which works in conjunction with the amygdala, is responsible for encoding information in Declarative “Cold” Memory (such as place, time, and contextual details). Under normal memory processes, these two structures work interactively. However, during a traumatic or stressful experience, the amygdala becomes hyperactive and blocks the functioning of the hippocampus.

In this case, the hippocampus cannot process elements of cold memory; instead, due to the excessive activation of the amygdala, elements of hot memory are intensely encoded and stored in the memory system. As a result, when a traumatic event is recalled, the sensations recorded by hot memory are activated, and the individual involuntarily re-experiences the bodily and emotional reactions felt during the event, such as trembling, heart palpitations, crying, and fear.

Due to the inability to encode information belonging to cold memory, the individual cannot remember contextual details of the event (such as place, time, and people). This leads to inconsistencies and fragmentation in autobiographical memory related to the traumatic experience, paving the way for the individual to experience PTSD symptoms (Schauer et al, 2024).

Due to this disruption in the structure of autobiographical memory, Foa and Kozak (1986) argued that reactivating fear networks is crucial to enable the healthy integration of information related to the event (elements of hot and cold memory) that were dysfunctionally stored by the amygdala and hippocampus. This integration is necessary for reducing PTSD symptoms and creating a coherent autobiographical narrative.

The reprocessing between memory systems occurs through repeated and safe re-experiencing of the traumatic event using the Imaginal Exposure technique. This method reduces avoidance of trauma-related cues and allows fragmented memories of the traumatic experience to be reconstructed in a healthy and coherent manner (Foa et al, 2019).

Based on these theoretical foundations, the aim of the NET technique is to create a coherent and integrated autobiographical memory, thereby enabling the healthy integration of the traumatic experience into the individual’s overall life narrative. For this reason, NET is concerned not only with narrating the worst events experienced but also with recounting significant positive life events (Katsounari, 2015)

Fundamental Principles of Narrative Exposure Therapy NET is specifically designed for individuals with PTSD who have experienced various types of traumatic life events and adverse experiences. Overall, it is structured around two core principles. One of these principles is the Testimony Therapy technique, which is a fundamental component of the therapeutic process.

In NET, this technique aims to “document all of the individual’s experiences in writing and provide this written account to the client at the end of therapy.” This shared product (the written document) created by the therapist and client during therapy allows the individual’s experiences to be heard by others, making the “silent scream” of trauma audible and shareable.

Furthermore, in many countries where this technique is widely used, this written document—a copy of the individual’s narrative—is accepted as legal evidence in court. Bearing the signatures of both the client and the therapist, this document also serves as a form of “human rights advocacy” (Schauer et al, 2025). Thus, the therapeutic process fulfills a meaningful purpose not only individually but also socially and politically (Weine et al, 1998; Bichescu et al, 2007).

The other component, the Exposure method, uses the “confrontation” technique to reorganize sensory processing related to traumatic experiences and place them into a functional context, aiming to reduce PTSD symptoms. The common goal of both techniques is to reconstruct the individual’s life in a functional and chronological manner, thereby reorganizing autobiographical memory (Schauer et al, 2024).

NET, which is based on the narrative technique, incorporates the universal pattern of “storytelling”—a method considered a shared heritage of humanity and cultures and passed down through generations. Although individuals with PTSD often struggle to articulate their experiences, the sense of relief that occurs after narration and the healing mechanism inherent in the narrative technique are regarded as fundamental components of NET (Schauer et al, 2005).

The inability to integrate traumatic experiences into one’s life story in a healthy way is one of the most common difficulties observed in individuals with PTSD (Brewin, 2014). In NET, all events experienced by the individual (both positive and negative) are addressed one by one and placed into a chronological context from birth to the present.

Moreover, the approach emphasizes that, alongside traumatic and adverse experiences, positive experiences also exist, and that the “lost” past is actually part of the individual’s life and should be brought to light. In this way, the individual can view all positive and negative events holistically and draw strength from their experiences. NET, in this respect, is a humanistic approach (Robjant & Fazel, 2010).

Additionally, by employing acceptance, empathy, unconditional positive regard, and active listening skills, it also embraces the principles of the Client-Centered Psychotherapy school (Schauer et al, 2024). Therefore, NET is a comprehensive and unique therapeutic technique that integrates principles from Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, Humanistic Psychology, Gestalt Psychology, Narrative Therapy, and Testimony Therapy.

Application and Structure of Narrative Exposure Therapy Structure of NET NET is a short-term treatment approach with a flexible session structure. It has been applied across various settings and cultures and has played a significant role in the remission of PTSD (Neuner et al, 2004). Studies have also examined the number and duration of sessions required for effective treatment.

Findings indicate that the number of sessions varies depending on factors such as the type and severity of traumatic experiences and the intensity of PTSD symptoms. For example, in an experimental study conducted by Zang and colleagues (2013) with Chinese earthquake survivors, the intervention group received four NET sessions, each lasting 60–90 minutes.
Results showed that this brief technique led to significant improvements in PTSD, depression, anxiety, and overall mental health at the two-month follow-up.

The developers of the method, Schauer and colleagues (2024), stated that an average of 10 sessions, each lasting between 90 and 120 minutes and conducted weekly, is suitable for the effectiveness of NET. However, they also emphasized that this may vary depending on the nature of the individual’s trauma. For example, when working with refugee groups, at least four sessions are considered necessary, whereas for torture survivors, 8–12 sessions are deemed more appropriate.
Additionally, for KIDNET—the child version of NET—it is noted that fewer sessions are effective, considering that a child’s life timeline is shorter compared to adults (Schauer, 2005; 2024).

NET: Application Overview: Theoretically and practically, NET is structured around four main phases: 1) Diagnosis–Assessment and Psychoeducation, 2)Creating the Lifeline, 3)Narrating the Lifeline, 4)Re-reading.

Structuring NET sessions in advance (in terms of duration and number of sessions) around these four main phases is highly important. Typically, the first session begins with an assessment of the individual’s psychological state and the provision of psychoeducation.

After explaining the possible mental state the individual may be experiencing, an explanation about the universality of human rights (for trauma and abuse survivors) is provided, demographic information is collected, medical and psychiatric history is taken, a current status assessment is conducted, and the individual is informed about how the process will proceed.

In the second step, the priority is to establish a comfortable and trust-based relationship with the individual, as they may be reluctant to share life events in detail, and individuals with PTSD may feel confused. This process begins by laying out the lifeline (a thick rope is used) on a flat surface. Chronological information about events is collected without delving deeply into emotional experiences.

Individual characteristics and unique circumstances are noted during this stage. The information gathered here is highly important for referencing and addressing later in the session process. After the lifeline is created, each event is processed one by one in chronological order. The individual’s narrative is written down in detail after the session (a short version of the session).

In the next session, this written narrative is read to the individual, and any omissions or inaccuracies are corrected. Then, the session continues from where it left off. In the final session, the complete written document (covering all sessions) is read aloud to the client. Both the client and the therapist sign the written narrative. A copy of the signed document is given to the client, while another copy may be kept for scientific purposes if needed.
Below, detailed information about the structured sessions is provided.

Session 1: Diagnosis, Assessment, and Psychoeducation Usually during the first session, or in some cases before the first session, the individual’s psychiatric history is identified, PTSD and any comorbid disorders are detected (for PTSD, it is generally recommended to use clinician-administered assessment tools such as the PTSD scale/CAPS-5). Then, problem areas are framed, detailed information about the individual is gathered, and treatment goals are established.
After diagnosis and assessment, the individual is asked if they have any questions. If they do, these are answered; if not, the session proceeds to psychoeducation.

In psychoeducation, the individual is informed about their current situation, it is emphasized that they are not alone, and their experience is “normalized” (they are told that experiencing such symptoms as a result of negative life events is normal).

Additionally, information is provided about possible symptoms (especially those related to PTSD, such as depression, stress, anxiety, insomnia, lack of enjoyment in life, self-devaluation, feelings of emptiness, and communication/family conflicts).

The intensity and content of psychoeducation should be tailored to the individual’s needs. For example, when working with a child, it is more effective to use words that children can understand and are familiar with, and, when necessary, to explain concepts through drawings, toys, or metaphors.

In addition, for individuals who may have difficulty using the language—such as refugees—it is very important to use an interpreter or to provide psychoeducation according to the person’s educational level (Schauer et al, 2024).

The purpose of psychoeducation is to help the individual understand, explain, and normalize their experiences, and to accept that their current situation is a result of traumatic experiences. In other words, it aims to provide information about dysfunctional emotions, thoughts, and behaviors, raise awareness, normalize reactions (emphasizing that these reactions and behaviors are understandable), and foster realistic acceptance.

Therefore, while providing explanations, all questions should be answered without causing confusion. Toward the end of psychoeducation, the process is discussed; explanations are given about the number of sessions, their duration, and structure, and the session is concluded.

Session 2: Creating the Lifeline After psychoeducation, the second session is dedicated to creating the lifeline. The lifeline is an essential component of NET and has become one of its symbolic elements. This line ritualizes and symbolically represents the person’s life story (Schauer et al, 2025). The lifeline is depicted using a rope or ribbon that represents the continuous flow of time.

It is usually created by placing a closed ball of yarn—symbolizing the ongoing nature of life—on a flat surface and stretching it out. The lifeline is placed on the ground by the individual, which encourages them to take control of their life during its creation. Then, the individual’s birth is marked at the very beginning of the lifeline using a symbol. At this point, symbols that are integral to NET are used. These symbols consist of flowers and stones.

Flowers represent positive, happy, and successful moments in the person’s life, while stones symbolize painful, negative, and traumatic life events. In some cases, additional symbols such as candles and pieces of wood or twigs may be used. A candle can represent situations such as the death of a loved one or a pet and the associated grief, while a piece of wood or twig can be used to distinguish situations where the person has experienced or perpetrated violence.

The developers of NET recommend not diversifying the types of symbols (such as using toys or personal items) and advise that the lifeline should be created within this framework. However, they suggest varying the qualitative characteristics of the flowers, stones, candles, and twigs. For example, larger and darker stones can be used for more traumatic experiences, while large and brightly colored flowers can represent highly joyful life events.

This way, life events can be easily distinguished from one another qualitatively.Y The symbol chosen to represent the individual’s birth is placed at the very beginning of the lifeline. However, if there was a major life event before birth that affected the individual or their family (such as relocation, changes in economic status, the loss of a family member, or illnesses in the family), and the individual considers it important, the lifeline can begin with these events.

The individual then places symbols representing all positive and negative experiences in their life from birth to the present, thereby creating the lifeline. When placing symbols on the lifeline, contextual information about the events is gathered without going into too much detail. Information related to location (such as city, home, school, street) and time (year, month, day, season, time of day, or parallel life events) is collected.
The individual is asked to label or name these with one or two words. However, since the goal here is not to expose the person to the event, these details are noted next to

the symbols only for later reference and recall. The lifeline ends chronologically with the present time. The individual and therapist then review the gestalt as a whole. At this point, it is important to acknowledge and appreciate the work done (Schauer et al, 2024). Completing this process within a single session and not carrying it over to the next is highly important.

Session 3: Narrating the Lifeline The next session begins with narrating the first event (symbol) on the lifeline. Since the lifeline usually starts with birth, as much information as possible is gathered about the individual’s family and the environment in which they were born. Then, the process continues chronologically by moving to the next symbol. The amount of time spent on each symbol depends on the significance of that event for the individual.

However, discussing positive and pleasant events should not exceed 15 minutes, while negative and traumatic experiences should be allocated as much time as necessary. Before talking about the event itself, contextual information should be clearly explained and elaborated: Time and place: When did the event occur? Life stage, time of year, time of day, a specific moment in the day.
Location and action: Where was the person? Where did the event take place? What was the person doing at that moment? What were they about to do?
Beginning: Detailed information about the start of the event (Schauer et al, 2024).

During the narration of the event (especially a traumatic one), the clinician and the individual switch to “slow-motion mode.” The person is asked to visualize the beginning of the event in their mind. From this point onward, the event is processed in detail, step by step. It is important to help the individual understand what they perceived.

As many questions as possible are asked about physical sensations, thoughts, behaviors, and details such as the shape, color, smell, and sound of objects, and the individual is encouraged to share this information. This approach reactivates sensory and emotional experiences related to the event, allowing associative memories to surface and cues to be uncovered through reminders. Reality is reinforced.
However, the most critical point is to prevent avoidance, dissociation, and flashbacks. While exposure and reliving are desired processes in therapy, dissociation is dangerous and should be avoided.

Therefore, it is essential to reinforce the individual’s presence with the clinician in the “here and now.” After reliving the event, placing it back into the context of the rest of the day and integrating the pieces is important for maintaining the integrity of autobiographical memory (Schauer et al, 2025). For example, if the event occurred in the afternoon, obtaining information about what the person did during the remainder of the day is crucial.

During the narration of traumatic and negative experiences, it is important to vividly evoke emotional and sensory memories. The goal of this evocation is to activate sensory, cognitive, emotional, and physiological components related to the event and integrate them. This integration ensures that the activation of one component triggers the activation of others, facilitating the healthy integration of “hot” and “cold” memory.

In this way, the autobiographical memory associated with the traumatic experience is reprocessed in a coherent and functional manner. To achieve the integration of hot and cold memory, questions targeting elements of the traumatic experience are exemplified in the NET manual by Schauer and colleagues (2025).Bu çalışma oturumun sonunu getirir. Oturumdan sonraki birkaç günde yaşanılanlar ve anlatılanlar üzerine ciddi düşünme ve içgörü kazanma süreci olabilir.

Bu bilişsel yeniden yapılandırma sürecinin doğal bir parçasıdır. Terapist oturumdan sonra hemen bireyin anlattıklarını ve hissettiklerini (oturum sırasında not almalıdır) tüm detayları ile kağıda dökerek onun bakış açısıyla yazmalıdır.

Session 4 and Beyond: Continuing the Narrative At the beginning of each session, the client should be asked how their week has been, what mood they are in, and what they think and feel about what they have shared so far. This allows for the identification of cognitive changes that may have occurred during the week and the recall of new details related to the reprocessing of autobiographical memory. The individual may also come with new insights about the event.

After this, the narrative written down by the therapist in the previous session is read aloud to the client. The client is asked to listen carefully and visualize what is being read. If necessary, changes or corrections are made, and the narration continues with the next symbol on the lifeline. All sessions proceed in this manner until the final session.

Final Session: Rerading the Narrative Starting from the first narrative session, the entire written document containing the individual’s narrative is read aloud to the client. If they wish to make any corrections or additions, these are allowed. One copy is given to the client and one to the therapist, and both sign the document. This joint signature and agreement on the truth of what has been narrated is the core component of Testimony Therapy.

However, it should be noted that in some cases, individuals with traumatic experiences (especially survivors of sexual abuse and neglect) may not want to keep a copy of this document and may prefer to leave these painful events behind and start a new chapter in life. In such cases, it is crucial to respect the individual’s consent and wishes.

As previously mentioned, this written document can serve as legal evidence in Europe and various parts of the world, as it is prepared under the supervision of a clinician for the purpose of human rights advocacy.

Following a successful intervention, the individual becomes someone who can think more functionally, socialize, evaluate new opportunities, has increased self-acceptance and awareness, knows their strengths, experiences reduced guilt and reluctance, has greater motivation toward life, and develops a belief in a safe world (Schauer et al, 2005; Mørkved et al, 2014; Schauer et al, 2025).

The Role of the Therapist in Narrative Exposure Therapy In the NET technique, the individual is encouraged to narrate events in as much detail as possible, particularly to ensure the integration of sensory and contextual information. This allows the person to re-experience the sensory, cognitive, and emotional components of the memories (Mørkved et al, 2014).

This is because, for the healthy integration and chronological flow of autobiographical memory, two core principles of NET are essential: helping the individual relive the event (exposure) and reinforcing their sense of safety in the here and now (habituation).

Considering that individuals with PTSD often have distorted perceptions of themselves and the world, along with reduced functionality in daily life, the therapist carries significant responsibilities stemming both from the sensitivity of the NET technique and the nature of trauma (Robjant & Fazel, 2010).

Fundamentally, respect must be shown to the individual and their experiences throughout the narrative. This respect and acceptance should be combined with empathy and verbally reflected when necessary. However, two important points must be considered. Firstly, if there are inconsistencies in the individual’s narration during therapy, these should be gently and appropriately addressed using proper interviewing skills—even though it represents the person’s reality.

Secondly, while showing acceptance and empathy, the therapist should avoid glorifying or heroizing the individual. Since people with PTSD often have endured extremely difficult life events, therapists may sometimes respond in an overly admiring way. However, this can prevent the individual from later sharing shameful or self-deprecating experiences, as they may fear shattering the “heroic image” perceived by the therapist.
It is also important to avoid artificiality and to provide appropriate and measured responses.
Due to the nature of traumatic experiences, it is quite normal for individuals to experience difficulties such as being unable to speak or express themselves verbally (Schauer et al, 2024).

Therefore, the therapist may occasionally use certain encouraging interviewing techniques to help the client express themselves verbally. However, it is still important that the therapist does not interpret or speak on behalf of the individual. The person themselves is the one who truly knows what they have experienced and felt.

There should be no judgment regarding what is right or wrong; the individual’s own reality should be accepted from their perspective and should not be corrected. Additionally, individuals with traumatic experiences often express their silence through bodily reactions (such as rubbing their hands, crying, trembling, sweating, rapid breathing, and feeling restless).

In such cases, providing feedback about these bodily reactions can both increase the individual’s awareness and allow them to feel that the therapist is present, values them, and understands them throughout the process.

Throughout NET sessions, the therapist must ensure they understand what the individual is saying. They should not skip over points they do not understand, but instead clarify confusion by appropriately stating that they need an explanation. For example, a phrase such as “I didn’t quite understand what you said.
Could you repeat that?” (Schauer et al, 2024) helps eliminate confusion and shows the individual that efforts are being made to understand them, which prevents feelings of loneliness.

As mentioned above, narrating traumatic experiences in as much detail as possible is crucial for the functional reintegration of autobiographical memory. Therapists who are new to the NET technique often report difficulty in eliciting detailed accounts (Robjant & Fazel, 2010; Schauer et al, 2011).

The key to overcoming this challenge is for the therapist to visualize what the individual is describing as if it were a film, correcting inconsistencies and filling in gaps by asking questions. This approach helps the therapist form a more concrete mental image of the event while simultaneously encouraging the individual to provide a more detailed narrative. In other words, the imagination technique works in a reciprocal manner.

The therapist should avoid behaviors that could harm the narrative process and act honestly and predictably. Especially when working with individuals with PTSD, building and maintaining trust is essential. The therapist should adopt a genuine and warm attitude and provide flexibility when necessary. For example, if the individual wishes to discuss an important event that occurred during the week, they should not be dismissed, and sufficient time should be allocated.

However, this should not dominate the entire session. Since NET is a structured technique, the individual should be informed about the process before the session and whenever necessary, ensuring no confusion arises. In some cases, the therapist may express understanding by sharing limited personal information, but this is generally not recommended.

During the narrative process, the therapist should avoid talking about themselves (except in very limited cases), making random comments, adopting a didactic attitude, giving advice, and should remain aware of their posture and reactions. For example, they should be careful not to display reactions such as deep sighing, disgust, or laughter (Schauer et al, 2025).

Additionally, the therapist should remain predictable in their actions and, if they need to perform any behavior during the session (such as adjusting a chair, drawing a curtain, or closing a door), they should explain this to the individual beforehand.

As with other therapeutic processes, NET is subject to the highest standards of confidentiality and commitment between the individual and the therapist. Therefore, it is essential to provide assurance and emphasize that no information will be shared with third parties without the individual’s consent. Since this process is built on principles of trust and confidentiality, the individual’s voluntary participation is fundamental.

Although individuals with PTSD may fear that their experiences will not be understood or cannot be expressed, they should be encouraged to share their narrative. On the other hand, if the individual does not wish to talk about their experiences, the therapist must always respect their boundaries, avoid overwhelming them, and never pressure them to disclose.
However, the therapist should also inform the individual about possible consequences and responsibilities (Schauer et al, 2024).

Different Forms of Narrative Exposure Therapy Although the NET technique was originally developed for the treatment of PTSD in adult refugee populations, over time it has been applied to different populations and various adaptation studies have been conducted.

The version of NET developed for children and adolescents is called KIDNET. The first studies were based on clinical trials conducted with outpatient child patients at the University of Konstanz and research with displaced children in Sri Lanka. The results of these studies demonstrated that KIDNET is particularly effective for children who have been displaced or are victims of organized crime (Schauer et al, 2004; Onyut et al, 2005).

Unlike adults, building trust is even more critical in KIDNET. The goal is to restore emotional connection through therapeutic interaction while addressing attachment issues caused by traumatic experiences.

To establish this trust, visual materials such as drawings and figures may be used during lifeline creation or narration. Creativity and play can be highly beneficial for helping children elaborate their narratives. In this context, Schauer et al (2024) emphasize that creating the lifeline is of critical importance in KIDNET. The creativity involved in this process can help children overcome barriers and express themselves more comfortably.

Compared to adults, children’s lifelines may be shorter depending on age; however, in some cases, they can be nearly as long as an adult’s. Additionally, in KIDNET, the lifeline can be enriched with symbols representing not only the past but also the future. For example, life events such as “When I finish school” or “When I get married” can be placed on the lifeline using appropriate symbols (Schauer et al, 2024).

The version of NET for offenders is called FORNET. In addition to the core principles and components of NET, FORNET focuses on “the perpetration of violence.” Its aim is to help offenders gain control over violent behaviors (Crombach et al, 2015).

Alongside KIDNET and FORNET, in response to the restrictions brought by the COVID-19 pandemic, Kaltenbach and colleagues (2021) developed the online version of NET, known as e- NET, and published a manual for its implementation.

NET also has versions tailored for traumaaffected older adults (ElderNET) and for communities exposed to collective trauma (such as villages, ethnic groups, or families), where individual trauma narratives are processed within a group setting—this version is called NETfacts (Schauer et al, 2025).
The Effectiveness of Narrative Exposure Therapy in Treating PTSD and Comorbid

Disorders NET was originally designed and implemented by Schauer and colleagues (2005) to treat psychological problems among refugee populations living in post-conflict regions. As a short-term and effective therapeutic technique, it was rapidly adopted worldwide and its research scope has expanded significantly.

The first experimental study investigating the effectiveness of NET was conducted by Neuner and colleagues (2004) with 43 Sudanese refugees settled in Uganda. This study, carried out between 2000 and 2001, involved 43 Sudanese refugees who had fled the civil war and settled in northern Uganda. Participants were randomly assigned to three groups: The first group (N = 12) received only one session of psychoeducation.

The second group (N = 14) received psychoeducation plus three sessions of Supportive Counseling. The third group received psychoeducation plus three sessions of NET. The researchers conducted the study with the help of local interpreters and collected data at four different time points. Pre-test, post-test, and follow-up assessments at 4 months and 1 year revealed significant differences between the groups. The group that received NET showed a
